blocks.text: We will examine hydrogenation and halogenation addition reactions of benzene in the following reactions.

The hydrogenation of benzene and other arenes, involves the addition of 1, 2, or 3 moles of hydrogen to the carbons of benzene. Cyclohexane is produced when benzene is completely hydrogenated. Cyclohexane is a useful solvent and a precursor in the production of other chemicals.

blocks.alt: Benzene + 3H2 gives cyclohexane, a ring of six CH2 groups. Methylbenzene + 3H2 gives methylcyclohexane, a ring of one CH carrying CH3 and five CH2 groups.
blocks.caption: Hydrogenation of benzene and methylbenzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 70).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed methylcyclohexane shows the ring carbon that carries CH3 as CH2, which would give that carbon five bonds; it is CH, as drawn above.

These reactions destroy the electron delocalisation in the original benzene ring, because those electrons are being used to form bonds with the new hydrogen atoms. Although the reactions are exothermic overall because of the strength of all the new carbon-hydrogen bonds, there is a high activation barrier to the reaction. The reactions are done using the same finely divided nickel catalyst that is used in hydrogenation of alkenes and at similar temperatures (around 150°C), but a higher pressure is applied.
Chlorine and bromine react in the same way. In the absence of a catalyst, UV light and heat are sufficient for complete halogenation. The complete chlorination of benzene is shown below:

blocks.alt: Benzene + 3Cl2, with UV, heat over the arrow, gives hexachlorocyclohexane: a six-membered ring of single bonds with one H and one Cl on every carbon.
blocks.caption: Complete chlorination of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 71).

blocks.title: Quick Check 20.8
blocks.text:
a) Predict the product formed when:
i. the compound given here is oxidized using acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇.
ii. Bromine is added to chlorobenzene in the presence of AlBr₃.
iii. Nitrobenzene is reduced in the presence of Ni at high temperature and pressure.

blocks.alt: A benzene ring with three groups at alternate carbons: an isopropyl group, CH(CH3)2, at the top, a CH3 at the lower left and a 2-methylpropyl group, CH2CH(CH3)2, at the lower right. Label: 3-isobutyl-5-isopropyltoluene.
blocks.caption: The compound of Quick Check 20.8 (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 71).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed name '3-Ethyl-5-propyloluene' does not match the drawing, which has an isopropyl group, a methyl group and a 2-methylpropyl (isobutyl) group; its name is 3-isobutyl-5-isopropyltoluene, as labelled above. The answer to the question is the same: benzene-1,3,5-tricarboxylic acid.
